title: Imports: Real Analysis, Algebraic Numbers, Linear Algebra
content: The import list reflects the multidisciplinary nature of Baker's theorem: real analysis (`Real.log`, `ExpDeriv`), complex exponentials, algebraic number predicates (`IsAlgebraic`, `Transcendental`), linear independence, and irrationality. Notably, `Mathlib.NumberTheory.Primes.Infinite` is imported for the primality facts used in the elementary irrationality proof of log₂(3).
mathContext: Baker's theorem sits at the intersection of transcendence theory (algebraic vs. transcendental), real analysis (logarithms), and algebra (linear independence over fields).

title: Module Header: Baker's Theorem Statement, History, and Proof Strategy
content:
The module header documents the full mathematical story of Baker's theorem. The statement — that Q-independent logarithms of algebraic numbers remain Q̄-independent — is presented in both homogeneous (no constant term) and inhomogeneous (includes β₀) forms. The historical timeline traces from Hermite (1873) through Lindemann (1882), Gelfond-Schneider (1934), to Baker (1966) and Baker-Wüstholz (1993). Baker received the Fields Medal in 1970, making this one of the most celebrated transcendence results in the 20th century.

The proof strategy is outlined: Baker's method constructs an auxiliary analytic function F with coefficients from Siegel's lemma, forces it to vanish at many points via an extrapolation argument using the hypothesis Λ=0, then derives a contradiction via the Schwarz lemma (an analytic function cannot vanish too often while staying bounded). This approach has been the dominant paradigm in effective Diophantine geometry since 1966.

The status checklist documents what is formalized (irrationality of log₂(3), Q̄-independence of {log 2, log 3}) vs. what remains as axioms (Baker's theorem itself — pending the analytic machinery).
mathContext: Baker's theorem: $\Lambda = \beta_1 \log \alpha_1 + \cdots + \beta_n \log \alpha_n \neq 0$ whenever $\log \alpha_1, \ldots, \log \alpha_n$ are $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent and $\beta_i \in \bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ are not all zero. Equivalently: $\mathbb{Q}$-independence implies $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$-independence.

title: Elementary Arithmetic: 2^p ≠ 3^q and Logarithm Positivity
content:
The arithmetic core of the irrationality proof is `two_pow_ne_three_pow`: if 2^p = 3^q then 2 divides 3^q, so by `Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow` (since 2 is prime), 2 divides 3 — a contradiction. The proof uses `dvd_pow_self 2 hp.ne'` to get 2 | 2^p, then `heq ▸ h2dvd2p` to transfer to 3^q.

This is the unique factorization argument in disguise: the prime factorizations of 2^p and 3^q involve completely disjoint prime sets ({2} vs. {3}), so they cannot be equal. The Lean proof is more parsimonious, using only primality of 2 rather than the full fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

The helper lemmas `log_two_pos` and `log_three_pos` use `Real.log_pos` (log x > 0 iff x > 1) and `norm_num` for the numerical conditions 2 > 1 and 3 > 1.
mathContext: Key: if $2^p = 3^q$ then $2 \mid 3^q$ hence $2 \mid 3$ (primality), contradiction. $\log 2 > 0$ since $2 > 1$; $\log 3 > 0$ since $3 > 1$.

title: Irrationality of log₂(3) and Q-Linear Independence of {log 2, log 3}
content:
`log2_3_irrational` proves log 3 / log 2 ∉ ℚ without any transcendence theory. The proof: if log 3 / log 2 = p/q ∈ ℚ (with q = rat.den, p = rat.num), then q · log 3 = p · log 2, so log(3^q) = log(2^p), hence 3^q = 2^p by injectivity of log on positives. This contradicts `two_pow_ne_three_pow`. The proof carefully handles sign: since log 2, log 3 > 0 and d > 0, the integer n = p must be positive, enabling the cast from ℤ to ℕ.

`log2_log3_rat_indep` deduces Q-linear independence of {log 2, log 3}: if c₀ log 2 + c₁ log 3 = 0 with c₀ ≠ 0, then log₂(3) = log 3 / log 2 = -c₀/c₁ ∈ ℚ, contradicting irrationality. The proof handles both cases (c₀ ≠ 0 and c₁ ≠ 0) symmetrically.

Note: This is the prerequisite for Baker's theorem (the logs must be Q-independent before Baker gives Q̄-independence). The elementary irrationality proof stands independently of Baker.
mathContext: If $\log_2(3) = p/q \in \mathbb{Q}$, then $3^q = 2^p$, contradicting unique factorization. Q-independence: if $c_0 \log 2 + c_1 \log 3 = 0$ and $c_1 \neq 0$, then $\log 3/\log 2 = -c_0/c_1 \in \mathbb{Q}$, contradiction.

title: Baker's Theorem Axioms: Three Forms of the Main Result
content:
Three axioms encode Baker's theorem at increasing levels of strength. `baker_homogeneous`: the pure form, no constant term — Q-independent logs give Q̄-independent logs (any algebraic linear combination is nonzero). `baker_inhomogeneous`: includes an algebraic constant β₀, requiring Q-independence of {1, log α₁, ..., log αₙ}. `baker_quantitative`: explicit lower bound B^{-C} for the linear form with integer coefficients bounded by B.

In Lean, Baker's theorem is stated as an `axiom` — a declaration with no proof body, asserting the statement as an unverified assumption. This is mathematically honest: the proof requires substantial analytic machinery (Siegel's lemma + auxiliary functions + Schwarz lemma) that is not yet formalized in Mathlib. Using `axiom` rather than `theorem ... := sorry` makes the assumption explicit and uncancellable.

The docstrings carefully document WHY the inhomogeneous form is strictly stronger than the homogeneous form, with the example 2 log 2 - log 4 = 0 (which is *not* excluded by the homogeneous form since log 2 and log 4 = 2 log 2 are Q-dependent).
mathContext: Baker (homogeneous): $\sum_{i=1}^n \beta_i \log \alpha_i \neq 0$ for algebraic $\beta_i$ (not all zero) and $\mathbb{Q}$-independent $\log \alpha_i$. Baker (quantitative): $|\sum b_i \log \alpha_i| > B^{-C}$ for integer $b_i$ with $\max|b_i| \leq B$.

title: Corollaries: Transcendence of log₂(3) and Q̄-Independence of {log 2, log 3}
content:
`log2_3_transcendental` derives transcendence of log 3/log 2 from Baker. Assume β = log₂(3) is algebraic. Then β · log 2 + (-1) · log 3 = 0 with algebraic coefficients (β, -1) and Q-independent logs (log 2, log 3 are Q-independent by log2_log3_rat_indep). Baker gives this sum is nonzero — contradiction.

The Lean proof carefully constructs the Fin 2 indexed families α = ![2, 3] and βc = ![β, -1], then assembles the Baker hypotheses (positivity, algebraicity, Q-independence). The final step uses `div_mul_cancel₀` to show β · log 2 = log 3 and `ring` to close.

`log2_log3_alg_indep` is the direct application of Baker to prove Q̄-independence: for any algebraic β₁, β₂ not both zero, β₁ log 2 + β₂ log 3 ≠ 0. This strengthens `log2_log3_rat_indep` (only Q-coefficients) to Q̄-coefficients — the key upgrade from Baker.
mathContext: Transcendence: if $\beta = \log_2 3$ is algebraic, then $\beta \log 2 - \log 3 = 0$ contradicts Baker. $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$-independence: $\beta_1 \log 2 + \beta_2 \log 3 \neq 0$ for algebraic $\beta_i$ not both zero.

title: n=1 Case (Gelfond-Schneider Corollary) and Four Exponentials Conjecture
content:
`baker_n1_log_independence` proves the n=1 case of Baker: if α ≠ 1 is a positive algebraic number and β is a nonzero algebraic, then β · log α ≠ 0. This is immediate since a single nonzero vector is always Q-linearly independent. The Lean proof establishes `Fintype.linearIndependent_iff` for the singleton family `fun _ : Fin 1 => Real.log α`, then applies `baker_homogeneous 1`.

This implies a version of Gelfond-Schneider: log α is not annihilated by any nonzero algebraic number. The connection is: Gelfond-Schneider says α^β is transcendental (i.e., β · log α ∉ (2πiℤ)) for irrational algebraic β; Baker's n=1 case says β · log α ≠ 0 for any nonzero algebraic β (a weaker but cleanly algebraic statement).

The Four Exponentials section (lines ~549-558) is pure documentation — the conjecture is stated but not axiomatized, as it is an open problem. It documents the known partial results: Six Exponentials Theorem (proved, implied by Baker), Five Exponentials Theorem (proved), and the open Four Exponentials gap.
mathContext: Baker $n=1$: $\{\log \alpha\}$ is always $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent (nonzero singleton), so $\beta \log \alpha \neq 0$ for nonzero algebraic $\beta$. Four Exponentials Conjecture (open): if $z_1, z_2$ and $w_1, w_2$ are each $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly independent, then at least one $e^{z_i w_j}$ is transcendental.

title: Baker-Wüstholz Theorem: Optimal Quantitative Lower Bounds
content:
`baker_wustholz_bound` states the 1993 Baker-Wüstholz theorem: if Λ = Σ bᵢ log αᵢ ≠ 0 (integer coefficients), then log|Λ| > -C(n,d) · Π log(Aᵢ) · log(B), where C(n,d) = 18(n+1)! n^{n+1} (32d)^{n+2} log(2nd). This improves Baker's original 1966 bound (which had log^{n+1}(B) in the exponent) to the optimal log(B) power. The constant C(n,d) depends only on the number n of logs and the algebraic degree d of the field generated by the αᵢ.

The main applications are: (1) Thue equations f(x,y) = m have all solutions bounded by an effective constant depending on f, m; (2) Mordell's equation y² = x³ + k has all integer solutions with |x|, |y| bounded by exp(exp(C·log k)); (3) S-unit equations have all solutions explicitly bounded.

This is stated as an axiom: the Baker-Wüstholz proof uses the multiplicity estimates of Wüstholz, which go beyond Baker's original auxiliary function method and involve commutative algebra and group varieties — advanced machinery not yet in Mathlib.
mathContext: Baker-Wüstholz (1993): $\log|\Lambda| > -C(n,d) \cdot \prod_i \log A_i \cdot \log B$ where $C(n,d) = 18(n+1)! \cdot n^{n+1} \cdot (32d)^{n+2} \cdot \log(2nd)$. This is the sharpest known bound for linear forms in logarithms.
